A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Drama research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Atari100k results for Drama, learning curves, and ablations of sampling, Mamba backbones, and model size.

after.justification: v2 retains original Atari100k results and adds smaller-model comparisons, expanded sampling experiments, grid-world prediction results, timing measurements, and reconstruction examples.

M1.justification: The Mamba-2 dynamics model, discrete VAE, actor-critic procedure, DFS sampling probabilities, and training losses remain unchanged. Clarified notation, explanations of parallel training, and Appendix A.5 pseudocode document the existing procedure rather than introduce a new method.

E1.justification: v2 adds a synthetic 5-by-5 grid-world trajectory-prediction task requiring geometrically and dynamically consistent token generation (Section 4.2.3). This substantially extends evaluation beyond Atari reinforcement learning. The 26-game Atari100k coverage remains unchanged; expanding its sampling ablation does not itself add a dataset.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's direct Mamba-1 versus Mamba-2 ablation, v2 evaluates standalone GRU and Transformer controls in the grid-world comparison and adds a Transformer control to timing experiments. These broaden the direct backbone comparisons substantially. Table 1 retains its original comparator membership.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 12M-parameter DreamerV3 comparison while retaining the original 200M comparison. New protocols evaluate grid-world sequences of 208 and 1664 tokens using reconstruction error, memory usage, and per-step training time, plus timing sweeps over training and imagination lengths. Existing Atari interaction budgets and documented Drama hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The DFS ablation expands from four games to all 26 Atari100k games. v2 also adds sequence-length comparisons, computational scaling analyses, and reconstructed-frame case studies investigating Breakout failures and differences from Pong. The existing model-size analysis is retained in Appendix A.3, rather than removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report five Atari seeds and use min-max learning-curve bands. v2 additionally reports grid-world errors as mean plus/minus standard deviation in Table 2 and explicitly identifies standard-deviation intervals in Figure 10. It does not establish an increase in repeated runs or specify their count for these new measurements.

E6.justification: Table 1 scores remain unchanged. New comparisons report normalized means of 105 versus 37 for Drama versus DreamerV3XS, and 105 versus 80 for DFS versus uniform sampling; the latter medians are 27 versus 28. Table 2 adds prediction, memory, and timing results, including Transformer out-of-memory at 1664 tokens. The Freeway sampling finding changes from a clear DFS advantage in v1 Figure 2 to scores of 15 for both methods in v2 Table 4. Backbone learning curves and qualitative reconstruction findings also add or revise reported results.

T1.justification: Appendix A.6 introduces mathematical constraints defining valid grid-world geometry and definitions of geometric and logical prediction errors, whose average forms the new evaluation metric. The existing SSM derivations, DFS formula, and loss equations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: Mamba-based model-based RL, competitive Atari100k performance with a small world model, Mamba-2 advantages, and DFS mitigation of imperfect-model learning. The conclusion also retains its qualification that Drama does not decisively dominate Atari100k.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of applicability and failure. Its DFS discussion attributes advantages to later-stage dynamics and opponent exploitation while acknowledging weaknesses in Breakout and KungFuMaster. Appendix A.7 connects Breakout failures to omitted balls and visual complexity, qualifying the autoencoder explanation as needing further investigation. Appendix A.8 adds the qualification that Mamba-2's training advantage depends on sequence length.

D1.justification: v2 adds training pseudocode, grid-world construction and error-calculation details, implementation attribution, and timing information specifying an NVIDIA RTX 2000 Ada Mobile GPU and Transformer KV caching. Existing architecture hyperparameters and losses are retained. The repository URL's capitalization change does not establish a change in resource availability.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Long Range Arena, DITTO, mamba.py, and Recall to Imagine, including a short discussion of the latter's SSM-based model-based RL. It also corrects the placement of the TWM-style sampling attribution. The broader related-work organization and first-Mamba-agent positioning remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Most foundational prose remains intact. v2 corrects terminology and notation, clarifies dynamics-model targets, rewrites the experimental overview and sampling discussion, and relocates the model-size subsection to Appendix A.3. It also introduces an editorial defect by duplicating the Experiments heading and introductory paragraph as Sections 3 and 4.

P2.justification: v2 adds grid-world illustrations and results, comparative learning-curve displays, reconstruction montages, and timing plots. The four-game DFS display becomes a full-benchmark appendix figure and table, while existing ablation plots are reformatted or relocated. Figure 6 introduces an incorrect Mamba-1/Mamba-2 legend despite its retained S-versus-XS caption and analysis.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a similar-size DreamerV3 control and direct measurements supporting computational-efficiency claims. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence through the smaller-model comparison, sequence-length experiments, and timing measurements. Full-benchmark DFS evaluation and reconstruction case studies also improve assessment of effectiveness and failure conditions. Limited setup details for new tests, the unexplained Freeway revision, duplicated Experiments text, and Figure 6's incorrect legend weaken reporting, but the added controls and diagnostic evidence provide a substantial net improvement.
